title: The First Counterattacks
subtitle: Counterattacks, broken communications and the widening northern war
author: R.G. Cruise
summary: Soviet armour could delay German formations without restoring the front. The fighting in Lithuania and Ukraine exposes the difference between a powerful local attack and a coordinated operation.
body:
An attack timed to the hour

At 5.50 on the morning of 23 June, Colonel Pavel Poluboyarov sent the Northwestern Front a report that contained both an ambitious counterattack and the explanation for its likely failure. He had visited the commanders responsible for the Soviet armoured response in Lithuania. One mechanized corps was to attack at eleven, the other at noon, the different starting times intended to bring their movements together. Yet the army headquarters that was supposed to coordinate them had no communications with either the front or the mechanized corps. Poluboyarov requested fighters, bombers, fuel and ammunition. The attack existed as a set of personal instructions before it existed as a functioning operation. [1] By 25 June, this was the central problem of Soviet resistance across much of the invaded frontier. The Red Army was counterattacking, sometimes with determination and considerable local force. It was not standing aside while German columns passed. But attacking formations had to find the enemy, reach their assembly areas and cooperate with neighbours whose whereabouts were uncertain. German commanders could therefore encounter a dangerous tank attack on one road while another formation continued advancing beyond it. The Soviet difficulties were organizational and physical as well as tactical: a tank that could defeat an opposing vehicle could still become useless for want of petrol, a passable crossing or an order that reached its crew in time. [2] The fighting around Raseiniai illustrates that distinction particularly well. Here the Soviet command tried to strike the flank of Army Group North’s advance and protect the retreat of its rifle formations. The attack imposed a real battle on German armoured troops, but it did not restore the front. In western Ukraine, a larger concentration of Soviet mechanized corps was still developing its own counterstroke. Meanwhile, the war was becoming open and unmistakable in Finland, and German conquest in Lithuania was already bringing organized anti-Jewish violence. These were connected developments, although they cannot be reduced to a single narrative of tanks racing east. [3] The atlas view for 25 June should consequently be read as an uneven military situation. The German reference sheet is explicitly dated to the evening. It shows the command’s assessment of penetrations and opposing formations, not the disappearance of every Soviet force behind the leading symbols. Its useful question is where the main operational dangers were developing, rather than which side possessed every village between two coloured lines. [4]

The roads through Lithuania

Field Marshal Wilhelm Ritter von Leeb’s Army Group North had three principal instruments. Georg von Küchler’s Eighteenth Army advanced on the Baltic side; Ernst Busch’s Sixteenth Army operated farther inland; Erich Hoepner’s Fourth Panzer Group supplied the mobile striking force between and ahead of them. Its two motorized corps followed different routes. Georg-Hans Reinhardt’s XLI Corps encountered the Soviet armour around Raseiniai and the Dubysa, while Erich von Manstein’s LVI Corps drove farther east towards the Western Dvina crossing at Daugavpils, also called Dvinsk. Their common purpose was to break the Soviet armies in the Baltic region and open the approach towards Leningrad. Their immediate experiences were already diverging. [5] The rivers explain much of the operational geometry. The Niemen lay near the opening battlefield; the Dubysa divided routes through central Lithuania; the Western Dvina offered a much larger defensive barrier farther northeast. German success depended on crossing these obstacles before Soviet forces could organize behind them. Soviet success required more than the survival of a bridgehead or a single division. It required withdrawing troops to reach a new line, headquarters to establish communications and reserves to arrive before the attackers converted a crossing into a route for their whole formation. Roads and bridges made that a race with a limited number of possible destinations. [5] Fyodor Kuznetsov commanded the Soviet Northwestern Front. Pyotr Sobennikov’s Eighth Army covered the northwestern part of the threatened area, with Vasily Morozov’s Eleventh Army farther south. Their deployment had already been disrupted by the initial German blows. Kuznetsov’s directive of 22 June identified the German penetration towards Tauragė as a threat to the Eighth Army and ordered the Third and Twelfth Mechanized Corps to intervene. The Twelfth was to turn against the flank and rear of the advancing Germans. The Third was to bring its Second Tank and Eighty-fourth Motorized Divisions towards Raseiniai, while leaving its Fifth Tank Division with the Eleventh Army. That qualification matters: the Third Corps was not entering this battle with all the formations listed under its name in a prewar inventory. [6] The order also assigned Sobennikov responsibility for coordinating the two corps and directed the air force to strike German concentrations. This was a combined operation in conception, with armour, aviation, antitank defence and the retreating infantry intended to support one another. Its weakness lay in the widening distance between that conception and the actual condition of the command system. The same directive was trying to prevent encirclement, arrange a counterattack and prepare positions east of the Niemen. Headquarters was already pursuing several urgent tasks with forces whose freedom of movement was shrinking. [6]

Raseiniai and the broken counterstroke

Poluboyarov’s report gives the counterstroke a more precise shape than the broad arrows usually drawn over Lithuania. Alexey Kurkin’s Third Mechanized Corps was to move west from Raseiniai towards the Tauragė–Šiauliai road, then turn southwest towards Tauragė and Tilsit. Nikolai Shestopalov’s Twelfth Corps was to advance southwest on the other side of that road. The intention was to bring converging pressure against the German penetration rather than simply send tanks forward wherever fighting could be heard. Poluboyarov had even arranged a coded coordination table. His chosen attack times, eleven and noon on 23 June, provide a contemporary benchmark against which the operation can be judged. [1] The surviving report does not establish that either corps met that timetable in the intended strength. On the contrary, it states that the army lacked the communications necessary to direct them. A plan dependent on simultaneous movement was being transmitted through an officer travelling between headquarters. The difficulty was not that Soviet commanders had forgotten coordination; they explicitly sought it. They could not reliably supply its practical requirements. Requests for air cover and replenishment were still requests, and the enemy was continuing to move while those arrangements were being made. [1] Around Raseiniai, Soviet heavy tanks made that incomplete attack tactically formidable. The German Sixth Panzer Division encountered vehicles against which some of its customary antitank weapons were inadequate. German battle groups had to combine heavier guns, manoeuvre and close action instead of assuming that their normal armament would settle every encounter. The best-known episode involved a KV tank blocking the Raseiniai–Šiluva road and interrupting contact between two German battle groups. Archival research by Alvydas Žardinskas places this incident within the division’s actual communications problem, correcting retellings that inflate it into the immobilization of an entire invading army. [7]

A famous encounter

One tank and the scale of a claim

A roadblock could be important without stopping Army Group North. The Raseiniai KV interrupted a particular German division’s communications and required repeated efforts to destroy it. That is a substantial tactical achievement. Expanding it into a halt imposed on every German formation removes the geography that makes the incident intelligible. [7]

The Soviet evening summary for 24 June is more revealing about the wider battle than any isolated duel. It claimed a major success for the Second Tank Division, including large German equipment losses, but also reported that the division was around Raseiniai without fuel. German reserves had arrived and were attacking. The front was considering delivering fuel by aircraft. The same report said that the effect of the Twelfth Mechanized Corps’ operations could not be felt and blamed Shestopalov’s inactivity. These are statements by an embattled headquarters, not findings from an impartial inquiry. The German losses cannot simply be accepted as audited totals, and the accusation against the commander must be read beside the earlier admission that communications were broken. [2] Taken together, the records establish a narrower but firmer conclusion. The planned concentration had failed to become a sustained, coordinated attack capable of restoring the front. Soviet armour could inflict disruption, but its own ability to move and replenish was deteriorating. Tactical power remained present in particular vehicles and groups of men while operational control was falling apart around them. By 25 June, that separation was allowing the Germans to contain dangerous resistance locally and continue their wider advance. [2] [4]

A retreat that could not move as one

The Northwestern Front’s reports show that the tank battle was only one part of a larger disintegration. On the Baltic coast, the Sixty-seventh Rifle Division was fighting around Liepāja, called Libau in German records. The front reported heavy fighting, bombing of the harbour, airfield and railway station, fires in the city and the loss of communications. Farther inland, units of the Eleventh Army had lost much of their equipment and were attempting to reorganize around Babtai, Jonava and Vepriai. The whereabouts of the 128th Rifle Division were unknown to front headquarters. Each of these statements describes a different condition; none can be represented adequately by saying that the Northwestern Front had simply vanished. [2] The report also followed a German motorized column moving towards Šiauliai after a breakthrough between Kražiai and Kelmė during the previous evening. That direction threatened the connections behind the Soviet troops fighting around Raseiniai. Elsewhere in the same army, part of the Eleventh Rifle Division was organizing a new defensive line while the rest had yet to arrive from Narva. The problem was therefore not only replacing losses suffered in battle. A commander might be expected to defend a position with a formation whose remaining components were still approaching from far away, while an enemy column was already turning the roads behind it into a battlefield. [2] Some formations were holding positions, some were moving, some were assembling for transport and others could no longer be contacted. That unevenness made the retreat especially dangerous. A commander who kept a road open for his own troops might not know that a neighbouring route had been cut. A headquarters could issue a sensible order based on a position already overtaken by events. Even a successful local defence might become untenable when German armour reached its rear. The front’s reports repeatedly distinguish known positions from additional information still awaited, a useful corrective to later maps that make every formation appear simultaneously visible. [2] The consequences became unmistakable immediately after the date of this study. At ten in the evening on 26 June, Kuznetsov ordered an effort to rescue the Second Tank Division, now described as encircled and without fuel. A strong tank battalion was to carry fuel and shells, approach unexpectedly through the German rear towards Raseiniai and enable the division to escape towards Šiauliai. The action was ordered for the following morning. This is evidence of the intended rescue, not proof that the necessary battalion reached the stranded formation or that the division emerged intact. It nevertheless shows how quickly the purpose of Soviet armour had changed: from cutting into the German advance to opening a passage for its own survival. [8] That later order must not be moved backwards onto the 25 June map. Nor should the German seizure of the Daugavpils bridges on 26 June be treated as an achievement already completed the previous evening. The point of keeping these dates separate is practical. While Reinhardt’s corps fought through the Raseiniai area, Manstein’s route offered a different opportunity towards the Dvina. The German mobile advance was composed of several moving parts. Soviet resistance against one of them did not automatically protect the crossings threatened by another. [5]

The larger armoured battle forming in Ukraine

Farther south, the counterattack problem appeared on a greater scale. Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South was advancing with Ewald von Kleist’s First Panzer Group, supported by Walter von Reichenau’s Sixth Army on the northern part of the sector and Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s Seventeenth Army farther south. Mikhail Kirponos’s Southwestern Front possessed substantial mechanized forces, but their locations, movements and changing assignments prevented them from becoming a single concentrated weapon at the moment of the German crossing. The geography of Lutsk, Dubno, Brody and the approaches from Lwów created opportunities to strike the German penetration from different directions. It also created long and congested routes along which those forces first had to arrive. [9] Kirponos’s order issued at Tarnopol at nine on the evening of 24 June specified an attack at seven the following morning. The Eighth, Fifteenth and Fourth Mechanized Corps were named in the intended operation, which was to defeat the German mobile grouping north of the Shchurovytse–Dmytriv–Mosty Velyki line and reach the Voynytsia–Mylatyn–Sokal area. One purpose was to avert the encirclement of Mikhail Potapov’s Fifth Army. The order required units to occupy their starting positions during the night and commanders to verify that subordinates understood their tasks. These were concrete instructions with a date and an hour, not a vague exhortation to counterattack. [10] The aviation arrangements were equally exact on paper. Reconnaissance was to identify targets before 6.50; the strongest opening air strike was to take place in the ten minutes before seven; successive attacks were to support the armour afterwards. Tanks would mark themselves with red rockets and folded white sheets, and aircraft would signal recognition by rocking a wing. Such details reveal both a serious effort at cooperation and the fragility of the methods available. A timetable this precise depended on formations arriving together, pilots finding the intended targets and tank units distinguishing friendly aircraft while already under pressure. [10] By late on 25 June, a new order prescribed another attack for the next morning. The Eighth and Fifteenth Mechanized Corps were again central, now joined in the wider design by the Ninth and Nineteenth under Potapov’s control southwest of Lutsk. Assembly was required by 4.30 and the attack by nine on 26 June. The target was the German grouping around Radekhiv, and the northern corps were to assist by attacking along the Lutsk–Brody railway. This revised programme is direct evidence that the intended result of the previous order had not been secured on its stated terms. It does not establish that nothing had happened on 25 June; it establishes that the desired coordinated defeat of the German force remained ahead rather than behind. [11]

Reading an order

White sheets do not prove air support arrived

The recognition signals in the 24 June order are unusually concrete evidence of how the Soviet command intended armour and aircraft to cooperate. They cannot establish how many supporting sorties reached the battle. An operational order records what headquarters wanted; the results require situation reports, unit records and evidence from the opposing side. [10]

The full consequences of these battles belong to the study for 1 July. On the 25th, the important comparison with Lithuania is already clear. Both fronts were trying to strike German mobile forces on their flanks. Both depended on corps whose arrival and communications were uncertain. Ukraine offered a larger and more sustained armoured response, but a greater number of tanks did not abolish the problems of timing, fuel and command. Its battles would develop over several days, and their outcome should not be imposed prematurely on the men receiving orders that evening.

Finland’s passage into open war

The northern war acquired another public turning point on 25 June when Soviet aircraft attacked targets in Finland. The American minister in Helsinki, H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld, reported a conversation that evening with Foreign Minister Rolf Witting. Witting said that Finland was again at war and that the government would make its position clear to the Diet. He also emphasized that Finland was no longer alone and referred to German assistance. The dispatch captures the Finnish government’s immediate presentation of the event, rather than a later reconstruction written after the outcome was known. [12] The air attacks were a real escalation, but they did not create German–Finnish military cooperation out of nothing. German troops were already deployed in Finland, and preparations for operations against the Soviet Union had been coordinated before Barbarossa began. The Finnish leadership sought to recover territory lost in the Winter War and pursued its own national objectives, while the German command sought strategic benefits against the Soviet north. Those aims overlapped sufficiently to produce military cooperation without making Finland’s war identical in every respect to Germany’s. The distinction helps explain Finnish decision-making; it does not make the prior preparations disappear. [5] It is therefore misleading to describe Finland on 25 June either as an uninvolved neutral suddenly discovering a war or as a country whose every military action had already begun simultaneously with the German crossing on the 22nd. Preparations, deployments, attacks, political declarations and major ground offensives had different dates. The Soviet bombing enabled the Finnish government to frame the conflict publicly as a renewed defensive war. Schoenfeld’s dispatch also shows that the government understood the strategic difference made by Germany’s participation. Both facts belong in the account, without allowing either to erase the other. [12] For the wider campaign, the immediate significance was the enlargement of the Soviet command’s obligations. Forces and attention had to be assigned across a northern theatre reaching far beyond the Baltic advance. Yet it would be equally inaccurate to paint that entire theatre as a single moving front on 25 June. The German reference sheet extends into Finland precisely because the military problem was geographically broad. Its inclusion of deployments should not be confused with proof that every planned offensive was already under way. [4]

Conquest and murder in Kaunas

While Soviet units struggled to withdraw through Lithuania, Jews in Kaunas faced a danger for which the operational maps provide almost no adequate language. In his subsequent report covering the period to 15 October, Einsatzgruppe A commander Walter Stahlecker described efforts to encourage local anti-Jewish violence while concealing German direction. His account identified the night of 25–26 June as a major pogrom and credited a Lithuanian group led by Klimaitis with carrying it out after prompting from a German advance detachment. The report’s vocabulary attempted to turn murder into an administrative achievement. Its explicit concern with making German involvement invisible is particularly important evidence. [13] Stahlecker’s figures are perpetrator claims, not a neutral census of the dead. His account also served to advertise his organization’s effectiveness to superiors. Those limitations do not make the document useless: they tell us which questions it can answer most securely. It demonstrates a policy of instigating violence, using local participants and managing how responsibility would appear. It does not justify treating all Lithuanians as perpetrators, nor does the involvement of local killers reduce the responsibility of the German security organization directing and encouraging the process. [13] The setting was a society recently subjected to Soviet occupation and repression. German propaganda and local antisemites converted anger at Soviet rule into accusations against Jews as a collective. That accusation was false, and it supplied no defence for murder. The prisoners, families and neighbourhoods attacked were not interchangeable with the Soviet government. Keeping this distinction explicit is necessary because the perpetrators themselves tried to blur it. Their claim to be eliminating a political enemy was part of the machinery of persecution. [13]

Evidence of concealment

A report that describes its own deception

Stahlecker wanted anti-Jewish attacks to appear locally initiated without visible German orders. A photograph of local perpetrators would therefore not, by itself, disprove German instigation. The report makes the management of appearances part of the evidence historians must examine. [13]

This violence was occurring during the opening military advance, not after a settled occupation had replaced it. The conquest of crossings and cities created the conditions in which security detachments could operate, recruit assistance and attack civilians. A Soviet tank crew’s difficulty obtaining fuel and a Jewish family’s danger in Kaunas were different experiences, with different immediate perpetrators and causes. They nevertheless belonged to the same invasion. An atlas that follows only the most advanced armoured symbol would miss much of what German progress was already making possible.

What the counterattacks changed

By the evening of 25 June, the Soviet counterattacks had demonstrated that German tactical superiority did not mean immunity from resistance. Armour could be checked, communications interrupted and individual German formations forced to fight hard for routes that a campaign map reduced to a line. The same evidence shows why such achievements did not amount to a strategic reversal. The Soviet attacks had not restored dependable communications, reopened the whole frontier or prevented German formations on other axes from advancing. The Northwestern Front’s own reports, with their mixture of local success claims, missing units and requests for fuel, are the clearest record of that contradiction. [2] There is no need to invent a German deadline for every town to measure this result. The documented Soviet attack hours and objectives provide a sufficient standard: the intended coordinated blows had not produced their assigned operational effect. On the German side, the larger objective of destroying Soviet forces before they could consolidate farther east remained in progress. Continued Soviet resistance complicated that task, but the armoured penetrations were still threatening the routes through which a coherent retreat would have to pass. [1] [11] [5] The next stage would reveal the cost of losing those routes on a much greater scale. In the central sector, German armour was closing towards Minsk while Soviet troops farther west tried to fight or march their way out. The encirclement of Minsk would not mean that resistance had ended. It would show how an army could continue fighting after it had lost the communications, supply and freedom of movement required to fight as a front.

sourceMethod: Numbered notes link to the source list and return to their first use. Page and document references accompany the relevant notes. German situation maps and staff reports are evidence of what German headquarters recorded, not an omniscient picture of the battlefield. Soviet operational records are cited from the General Staff’s published documentary collections, accessed in transcription; archival identifiers are those printed in those collections. Orders establish intentions; they do not by themselves prove execution. Postwar military accounts are checked against dated records and identified as retrospective. Place names follow familiar historical usage, with present-day equivalents where useful.
